Teacher Notes

AI literacy should be taught as both a practical skill and a civic responsibility. Help learners understand that AI systems are tools built from data, algorithms, and human design choices—not magic, not neutral by default, and not reliable in every situation. Effective instruction should combine hands-on use with critical evaluation: What is the system being asked to do? What data might it rely on? What could be inaccurate, biased, private, or unclear? Who is accountable for the outcome? Encourage students to compare AI outputs with trusted sources, identify limitations, and explain when human judgment is necessary. The goal is not fear or blind trust, but informed, responsible participation.

Lesson Plan

4

Grade/Level

Adaptable for secondary, postsecondary, adult learning, and workforce training.

5

Learning Goals

By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to:

  • Define AI literacy.
  • Identify common places where AI appears in daily life.
  • Explain basic AI-related ideas such as data, algorithms, machine learning, generative AI, and uncertainty.
  • Evaluate AI outputs for accuracy, bias, privacy, transparency, accountability, and need for human oversight.
  • Describe why AI literacy matters as a civic and workforce skill.
